title: Zephyrus - Latency economics & concurrency discovery
summary: Initial discovery to map Zephyrus's p95 latency targets, burst concurrency model, and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Covered token/sec benchmarks, streaming behavior, fallback strategies, security needs (KMS/SAML), and an ask for a short pilot + benchmark spreadsheet run.
topics: hosting mode tradeoffs (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
security controls: KMS, SSO, audit logs
next_steps: Redwood: share benchmark workbook link and baseline scripts
Zephyrus: provide 3 representative prompt sets and traffic pattern (burst + steady-state)
Schedule 1-week pilot window to run hosted baseline and a dedicated run
action_items: Alex Mercer: send benchmark spreadsheet and quickstart scripts (due 2027-08-16)
Emma Liu: share internal token distribution telemetry and SLAs (due 2027-08-18)
Samir Patel: propose pilot capacity configuration and rough cost estimate (due 2027-08-20)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-08-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Tan (Redwood SE) — Emma Liu (Zephyrus Head of Platform), Rohit Verma (SRE Lead), Lara Chen (ML Engineer)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call, then we wanted to understand your p95 goals and what your traffic looks like.
[00:18] Emma (Zephyrus): hi folks, thanks. we want to keep this pretty focused — primary ask is to understand if hosted meets our p95 targets for conversational streaming, and what the economics look like for a dedicated pool or private deploy.
[00:32] Samir (Redwood SE): great. before we jump in, two quick clarifiers — which model family are you evaluating and are you expecting streaming token-by-token or chunked responses?
[00:45] Lara (Zephyrus): we're testing an open LLM variant — roughly 13B, primed for multi-turn chat. streaming token by token is critical for our UI so p95 streaming latency matters.
[00:59] Rohit (Zephyrus): and we're seeing big burst spikes from our ingestion pipeline — short spikes to 600 concurrent streams for 30-90s, steady state around 40-60 concurrents.
[01:15] Jules (Redwood): ok that helps. for streaming p95 we usually measure two things: first-token latency and per-token throughput once the KV cache is warmed. are you trying to hit a p95 first-token SLA?
[01:31] Emma: yes, ideally first-token p95 < 400ms in our primary region. end-to-end for 8-12 token replies we'd like overall p95 under 1s but first-token is the key UX metric.
[01:47] Alex: perfect, that frames it. quick note: our hosted tier can hit sub-300ms first-token for certain model/hardware combos in our benchmark, but it depends on sequence length, quantization, and concurrency. dedicated gives more predictable tail behavior since the pool isn't noisy. private (VPC) can be tuned but has more ops overhead.
[02:08] Rohit: when you say sub-300ms, that's for what token length and hardware? i.e. 512 context and on A100?
[02:18] Samir: in our public benchmarks that was 13B quantized on A100-ish class or equivalent Ampere instances. important caveat: sequence length distribution matters — if you have long histories we see higher attention cost.
[02:32] Lara: our median seq len is small, like 80-120, but tails go to 600 in some support threads.
[02:41] Emma: and we do session pinning — some users have long histories and others are short. so a hybrid latency profile.
[02:50] Alex: noted. for your 600-concurrent 30-90s spikes, that points to either autoscaled dedicated pools with burst capacity or hosted with routing/fallback policies. can you share the traffic shape?
[03:06] Rohit: yes — we'll share a histogram. short answer: 70% under 150 tokens, 25% 150-400, 5% >400. burst is mostly short conversations but many simultaneous.
[03:20] Samir: sounds like prefix/KV cache will help a lot for the 70% bucket. we do automatic prefix caching on compatible models which reduces per-token compute and improves p95 throughput.
[03:32] Lara: is that enabled by default on hosted? any limits?
[03:37] Jules: hosting enables it by default for supported checkpoints; dedicated gives you more control (you can tune cache size and eviction). private can use customer-managed KVS but needs ops config.
[03:48] Emma: on security — we must use customer KMS for keys and SAML SSO for the console. also audit logs retention is mandatory for us. can Redwood support that in hosted?
[03:59] Alex: hosted supports KMS integrations and we have SOC2 logs; longer retention and HSM are in enterprise add-ons. Private/VPC gives you full control. i'll send the security packet.
[04:10] Emma: please. also curious about the fallback strategy when capacity is constrained — if hosted is 429-ing do you have automatic model fallback?
[04:22] Samir: yes we support routing policies — fallback to a cheaper quantized variant or to a lower-tier replica, and also cross-region fallback. but there's a tradeoff on output quality.
[04:36] Rohit: can you quantify quality drop for your quantized variants? we can't afford hallucination regressions on docs.
[04:44] Samir: we'll include eval numbers in the spreadsheet — typically top-1 accuracy on our internal evals drops 1.5-4% depending on quantization and model. we'd pair that with your regression tests.
[04:58] Lara: for benchmarking, what's the recommended approach? we prefer to run a baseline against hosted first, then a dedicated run.
[05:08] Jules: common pattern: 1) shared benchmark workbook + scripts (we'll provide locust/bench harness) 2) run a hosted 24-48h baseline replicating your burst profile 3) run a dedicated config sized to your 600-concurrent bursts with autoscale 4) optionally a private on-prem scale if you want to mimic air-gapped latency.
[05:29] Emma: timeline-wise we want a pilot in late August if possible.
[05:34] Alex: sounds doable. we'll send scripts today.

[06:10] Emma: a deeper question on p95 measurement — do you measure client-to-first-byte or server-side processing only?
[06:18] Samir: both; our p95 metrics in the console are end-to-end from request intake to first-byte for hosted. we can also surface server-side breakdown (queueing, kernel time, kv cache hits).
[06:30] Rohit: how granular is the tracing? e.g. do we get per-token time series to inspect token/sec drop-offs?
[06:38] Jules: yes, we have token-level timers in traces for streaming sessions and you can export traces to your observability. note sometimes transcription in logs shows kv as K-V cache, the telemetry is precise though.
[06:50] Lara: cost question — what's the delta between hosted per-token cost and dedicated committed capacity? we need back-of-envelope numbers.
[06:59] Alex: hosted is usage-based — per-token plus request overhead. Dedicated is committed GPU pool — unit $/token is much lower at scale but you pay for reserved capacity. rough rule: above sustained ~200k tokens/day with high tail requirements, dedicated often becomes cheaper. we'll model with your traffic in the spreadsheet.
[07:23] Emma: ok. can you explain how continuous batching affects latency under bursts? i've read that high batching increases throughput but hurts tail.
[07:34] Samir: continuous batching groups requests on the runtime up to a configured window. it improves GPU utilization but increases per-request queueing. we tune window and batch size to balance p95 SLO. in dedicated you can set stricter batch windows or provide more replicas to reduce queueing.
[07:54] Rohit: what about cold starts for models with large KV caches — if we spin up new replicas during a burst does that blow our p95?
[08:03] Jules: cold starts can add 100-400ms depending on the checkpoint and hardware; our autoscaler can prefer warm spare replicas to reduce this at cost. we can size pool to have warm capacity for expected spikes.
[08:18] Lara: can we pre-warm with synthetic traffic?
[08:21] Samir: yes, the pilot scripts include a warmup phase.

[09:05] Emma: let's talk target metrics: first-token p95 target 400ms, end-to-end for small replies 1s, concurrency spikes to 600 for up to 90s, resume to 50 steady. is that the right framing?
[09:19] Alex: yes. we'll aim to validate hosted can meet that in your region. if not, we'll size a dedicated pool and show the economics.
[09:29] Rohit: can dedicated give more predictable p95 at the same cost? i.e. same hardware but reserved vs multi-tenant hosted.
[09:38] Samir: predictability is the main win for dedicated — less noisy neighbors, dedicated batch formation per tenant, and you can set strict autoscaler rules. cost per token on dedicated will generally be lower if you utilize capacity.
[09:52] Lara: any differences in network/topology for private VPC? we have a strict egress policy and need private connectivity to our KMS.
[10:01] Jules: private VPC keeps traffic on your network via peering; you control egress and KMS/HSM. there's more ops overhead and we'd need to coordinate infra teams.

[11:00] Alex: quick aside — do you have regulatory constraints on data residency?
[11:05] Emma: EU data residency for EU customers; we prefer region pinning and want audit logs stored in EU.
[11:12] Alex: hosted supports region pinning and log routing to region. private gives you direct control for compliance.

[12:00] Rohit: hypothetical: if hosted fails over cross-region, is there an option to route a small percentage to a lower-latency cheaper model to keep the UI responsive?
[12:12] Samir: yes, that's a routing policy — canary shifts, percentage routing, or full fallback. but cross-region increases RTT which may harm p95.
[12:24] Lara: how do you measure the p95 of streaming once the stream is open? is it per-token or sliding window?
[12:33] Jules: we emit per-token latencies and sliding p95s per minute. for UI we find first-token and 95th percentile of first-10-tokens are most correlated with perceived snappiness.

[13:05] Emma: for the pilot, we want three runs: hosted baseline, dedicated-size run, and a quantized variant run. can you seed a quantized variant?
[13:15] Alex: yes, we can provision a quantized variant of the same architecture and include eval diffs. we'll also flag quality regressions.
[13:24] Rohit: and we need to measure token/sec during stall conditions — e.g. when the KV cache misses spike. can we capture that?
[13:31] Samir: absolutely — our traces sample KV hit/miss and compute time; pilot scripts will include artificial cache miss patterns.

[14:05] Lara: small nit — what do you call "KV cache" in the UI? i've seen labels like "K-V cache" or "kayvee" in old docs — just want to know what to look for.
[14:14] Jules: it's 'KV cache' in the console, but you'll see variants in older logs.

[15:00] Emma: what's the SLA we can aim for in hosted? are there published numbers for p95?
[15:09] Alex: our hosted SLA covers uptime and request availability, but p95 latencies depend on model and are listed in our performance profiles. dedicated SLAs can include latency targets as an add-on. we'll include a perf profile table in the workbook.

[16:00] Rohit: what telemetry do you export — can we push to Datadog/NewRelic?
[16:08] Samir: yes, metrics and traces export via OTLP; logs can stream to your logging backend.

[17:10] Lara: curious about multiplexing — do you multiplex small chat sessions onto the same request to the model or is each session a discrete request?
[17:22] Jules: sessions are discrete requests but runtime batching multiplexes requests for GPU efficiency; per-session ordering is preserved. multiplexing at the application layer is up to you.

[18:05] Emma: let's get concrete — what do you need from us to size the dedicated pool?
[18:12] Samir: token distribution, peak concurrency duration, regional distribution, and acceptable quality delta for quantized variants. also cost constraints if any.

[19:05] Rohit: for targeting 400ms p95 first-token, do you have a ballpark GPU count or instance type recommendation?
[19:13] Samir: ballpark is 1-2 A100-equivalent GPUs per 200-250 steady concurrent streaming sessions for low-latency configs, but this is very workload dependent. for spikes you'll want warm spare capacity or autoscale step-up policies.

[20:00] Alex: we'll produce a sizing doc with two configs: conservative (warm spares, low batch window) and economical (tighter warm pool, aggressive batching).

[22:00] Emma: any concerns about session affinity? our product pins a user to a replica to keep KV warm.
[22:08] Jules: session affinity is supported; dedicated makes affinity easier to guarantee. hosted supports it with sticky routing but large-scale affinity can increase resource fragmentation.

[24:00] Rohit: in the pilot, can we run synthetic bursts of 600 concurrency for 3 minutes repeatedly to emulate real traffic? we worry about autoscaler cooldowns.
[24:12] Samir: yes, we'll craft the pilot to include repeated short bursts and tune autoscaler cooldowns to mimic production.

[26:00] Lara: how transparent are per-route costs? can we get token-level cost by API key/route?
[26:10] Alex: yes, console breaks down token costs per key/route and you can export usage. dedicated can also provide per-instance cost breakdowns.

[28:00] Emma: on the security doc — please include SAML, KMS, audit log retention periods, and SOC2 evidence.
[28:09] Alex: will do.

[30:00] Rohit: hypothetical failure mode — GPUs overloaded, lots of queueing — will your runtime shed load gracefully?
[30:10] Jules: yes we have prioritization and graceful degradation: reject heavy background batch jobs, reduce batch window, or fail over a percentage of traffic to lower-cost model variants. these are policy-driven.

[32:00] Lara: question about model variants: how easy is it to pin a route to a particular quantization level?
[32:08] Samir: it's route-level config. you can pin model, quantization, and fallback policy per route.

[34:00] Emma: what's the expected ops coordination for private VPC — how long from contract to greenfield VPC deploy?
[34:11] Alex: typically 6-8 weeks for private VPC depending on onboarding windows and your infra team's availability. dedicated is faster — usually 2-3 weeks for reserved capacity.

[36:00] Rohit: any recommended mitigations for long-history sessions to reduce per-request overhead?
[36:08] Jules: prefix summarization, selective context trimming, and using an embeddings + retriever flow to avoid sending full history to the model. we can help with prompt engineering patterns.

[38:00] Emma: rounding up — show us the numbers and we'll pick pilot dates.
[38:06] Alex: we'll send the workbook and quickstart. can we lock a pilot window 2027-08-24 to 2027-08-31?
[38:15] Emma: that works for us.

[40:00] Alex: final recap — deliverables: benchmark workbook and scripts, perf profile table, security packet. Zephyrus to provide token distributions, sample prompt sets, and traffic histograms. pilot run late Aug. any other open items?
[40:19] Rohit: please include sample cost models for both 1-month and 12-month commits.
[40:24] Alex: noted.

[41:00] Emma: thanks everyone. quick note — our procurement folks will need an initial SOW with estimated costs.
[41:08] Alex: we'll include a high-level SOW after the sizing doc.

[46:00] Jules: thanks all, we'll follow up with the links.
[46:06] Emma: thanks. bye.

End of transcript.

References/links mentioned:
- Benchmark workbook (to be sent): https://redwood.example/bench/zephyrus-pilot
- Security packet (to be sent): https://redwood.example/security/enterprise-pack.pdf

Notes about transcript: occasional ASR mislabels (Redwood Dedicate vs Dedicated), K-V vs KV cache spelled inconsistently. conversational disfluency preserved.
